lecture.title: Physiology of Female Reproduction
golden_tip: Exam trap: ovulation occurs ~36 hours after the ONSET of the LH surge — not at its peak and not days later.
The luteal phase is constant at ~14 days; cycle-length variation comes from the follicular phase, so ovulation day = cycle length − 14.
Meiosis is arrested twice: prophase I from birth until puberty, and metaphase II from ovulation until fertilization.
Most germ cells are lost to atresia: ~7 million at 5 months' gestation → 1–2 million at birth → <400,000 at puberty → <500 ovulated.

concepts.title: Reproductive Organs and the Hypothalamic–Pituitary–Ovarian (HPO) Axis
concepts.summary_ar: يشرح هذا المفهوم الأعضاء التناسلية الأولية (الغدد التناسلية) ووظيفتها المزدوجتين في إنتاج الأمشاج والهرمونات الجنسية، ثم ينتقل إلى محور الوطاء–النخامى–المبيض: هرمون GnRH النبضي المكون من عشرة أحماض أمينية، والغونادوتروبينات FSH وLH، والستيرويدات الجنسية المبيضية، مع حلقات التغذية الراجعة (الإنهيبين والستيرويدات) التي تنظّم المحور بأكمله.

sections.heading: The Gonads: Primary Reproductive Organs and Their Dual Function
sections.body_text:
The gonads are the **primary reproductive organs**: the **testis in the male** and the **ovaries in the female**. The gonads perform two essential functions:

- **Gametogenesis** — production of the gametes: **ova in the female** and **sperm in the male**.
- **Secretion of sex hormones** — **TESTOSTERONE in the male**, and **estrogen (oestrogen) and progesterone in the female**.

These two functions — generating haploid gametes and secreting the sex steroids that govern the reproductive tract — are the defining properties of the gonads as primary reproductive organs; every other component of the reproductive system subserves them.
key_points: The gonads are the primary reproductive organs: testis (male) and ovaries (female).
Gonadal function 1 — gametogenesis: ova in the female, sperm in the male.
Gonadal function 2 — secretion of sex hormones: testosterone in the male; estrogen and progesterone in the female.

sections.heading: Reproductive Hormones: GnRH, Gonadotropins, and Ovarian Steroids
sections.body_text:
**Gonadotrophic releasing hormone (GnRH)** is a **10-amino-acid peptide** released from the **hypothalamus** in a **pulsatile fashion** into the **hypophysial portal circulation**. There it stimulates the release of the gonadotropins — **FSH** and **LH** — from the **anterior pituitary gland**, which act on the **ovaries** to produce the **sex steroids**: **estrogens from granulosa cells** and **progesterone from thecal cells**.

- **LH stimulates the corpus luteum (CL) to produce progesterone.**
- The ovaries also produce **gonadal peptides (activin, inhibin, and follistatin)** and **growth factors**.
- Among their other functions, these ovarian-derived factors **feed back to the hypothalamus and pituitary gland to inhibit** — or, **at the midcycle surge, to augment** — **GnRH and gonadotropin secretion**.
- The **ovarian steroids are also critical for preparing the endometrium for placental implantation if pregnancy ensues**.

This cascade — hypothalamic GnRH → pituitary FSH/LH → ovarian steroids and peptides — is the backbone of the menstrual cycle.
key_points: GnRH is a 10-amino-acid peptide secreted in a pulsatile fashion into the hypophysial portal circulation.
GnRH → FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary → sex steroids from the ovary (estrogens from granulosa cells, progesterone from thecal cells).
LH stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone.
Ovarian peptides — activin, inhibin, follistatin — and growth factors feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, inhibiting (or augmenting at the midcycle surge) GnRH and gonadotropin secretion.
Ovarian steroids prepare the endometrium for placental implantation if pregnancy ensues.

sections.heading: The HPO Axis Diagram: Signal Flow and Feedback Loops
sections.body_text:
The female reproductive axis is classically drawn as a **hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis diagram** in which arrows run downward from brain to gonad and back up as feedback:

- **Hypothalamus → pituitary:** the hypothalamus releases **GnRH**, which reaches the pituitary through the portal circulation.
- **Pituitary → ovary (positive stimulation, marked '+'):** **LH and FSH** act on the ovary (a cross-section showing follicles at various stages of development) to drive **follicular maturation**.
- **Ovary → uterus and systemic circulation:** the ovary releases **estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone** into the systemic circulation; these hormones act on the **uterus** (shown anatomically with fallopian tubes and ovaries).
- **Steroid feedback (– or +):** **estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone** feed back on the **hypothalamus and pituitary gland** with a negative — or, near midcycle, positive — effect.
- **Inhibin feedback (–):** **inhibin** released by the ovary exerts **negative feedback on the pituitary** (drawn as a red inhibitory arrow in the diagram).

Because the loop is closed, the hypothalamus and pituitary continuously monitor ovarian steroid and peptide output and adjust GnRH/gonadotropin secretion accordingly — this is the operating principle of the whole menstrual cycle.
key_points: HPO axis flow: GnRH (hypothalamus) → FSH/LH (pituitary, '+' stimulation) → follicular maturation and steroid output (ovary) → uterus.
Ovarian steroids (estrogen, progesterone, testosterone) feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary (negative, or positive at midcycle).
Inhibin selectively inhibits the pituitary (negative feedback).
